title: A historian says AI solved a 200-year-old mystery in just 22 minutes
excerpt: Historian Mark Humphries asked GPT-6.2 Astra to find the author of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook. It found a match in 22 minutes, he said.
content_html:
By Henry Chandonnet

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-25T19:27:36.152Z

AI is already solving the great mysteries of mathematics. History could be next.

Mark Humphries said that he used OpenAI's tools to find the origins of an anonymous sketchbook dating back to 1808. Better yet, he said it took the AI tool almost no time: 22 minutes.

Humphries is a professor of history at Wilfrid Laurier University in Waterloo, Ontario. He's studied the fur trade since the pandemic and has long been interested in an unnamed travel sketchbook held at Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library.

The problem: the sketchbook had some captions, few dates, and charted a path that thousands of travelers took.

Humphries is in a community of OpenAI users that gets early access to models for testing. So, he pointed GPT-6.2 Astra at the sketchbook's digital rendering, cranked it up to Ultra on goal mode, and asked it to find the origins.

The AI model used primary sources, such as a fur trader's dinner diary and a club's meeting minutes, to narrow down who could be in the sketchbook's locations. Eventually, it identified one man: Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot, vicomte de Chabot.

A human could do the same investigation, Humphries told Business Insider in a Wednesday phone call. But the documents GPT-6.2 Astra considered named hundreds of people, all of whom would need to be checked. That would make the process time-consuming, he said.

"Are you going to devote the years and years to doing that?" he asked. "The answer is probably no."

The AI also gave Humphries a path to prove its conclusion himself. Deep in a historian's Ph.D. dissertation, it found a reference to a diary Chabot kept, which he could order as microfilm copies.

Humphries found the handwriting of the diary and the sketchbook to look identical. It was interesting, sure, but not conclusive. "I'm not a handwriting expert," Humphries said.

Then there were the entries. The diary's dates lined up perfectly with the sketchbook, placing Chabot in "the right places at the right times," Humphries said.

And then, what could prove to be the smoking gun: In the diary, Chabot wrote that he made a sketch of Fort St. Joseph, and specified the view that he was looking at. In the sketchbook, there's the sketch of the same landmark with the same view.

"That's kind of the X-marks-the-spot kind of thing you don't typically find as a historian," he said.

How historians are feeling about AI

Mathematicians have had an emotional response to the rise of AI in their field. They hurled insults at an Anthropic staffer over a joke in a proof. Steven Strogatz wept on "The Daily."

Comparatively, the historians have been fairly chill.

They asked questions about Humphries' process and joked about the similarity of Chabot to "chatbot." A librarian at Yale that Humphries contacted received the finding warmly, though they've yet to do anything with the information, Humphries said. (Yale didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.)

Of course, the authorship of a niche sketchbook doesn't have the same implication as the Riemann Hypothesis. And some historians pointed out what Humphries himself said: that a human could do the same thing.

The biggest names in AI clearly see Humphries' finding as a win. OpenAI president Greg Brockman reposted him, celebrating the model's solution to a "significant historical mystery." Tech workers flooded his X comments with congratulations or statements of amazement.

For his part, Humphries doesn't think AI is equipped to do everything in history. "I'm much more ambivalent toward the technology than people think I am," he said. He doesn't use AI for writing, for example.

His goal, then, is to make sure historians know what they're getting into. As math goes through what some call a "crisis," Humphries said, historians should be clear about just what AI is good at.

"There are real limitations to the technology," he said. "What I'm trying to do is point out a thing that the models are capable of doing."
